_readme: ESL -> Native rule pack. Deterministic L1-transfer patterns that generic grammar checkers miss. Each rule names its first-language cause.

esl.title: Missing article (Chinese has no 'a/an/the')
esl.why: Chinese has no article system, so 'a/an/the' get dropped entirely. This is the single most reliable L1 tell of a Chinese native speaker.
esl.fix: Add the article: 'I am a student', 'he is an engineer', 'in university'.

esl.title: Measure-word / plural-noun leak (Chinese classifier habit)
esl.why: Chinese uses a measure word between number and noun (three 'students') and often keeps the classifier in English, producing 'many peoples' / 'three years of experiences'.
esl.fix: Drop the classifier: 'many people', 'three years of experience'.

esl.title: 'De'-style nominalization (Chinese often stacks nouns)
esl.why: Chinese can stack modifiers and nominalize densely. The result reads to English ears as an unnaturally dense noun pile.
esl.fix: Unstack into a clause: 'problems with punctuation' not 'punctuation problems analysis improvement'.

esl.title: Tense drift (Chinese verbs carry no inflection)
esl.why: Chinese verbs do not conjugate for tense/pers. Writers keep present tense where English requires past -- very visible in application essays.
esl.fix: Use past tense: 'Last year I worked at...' not 'Last year I work at...'.

esl.title: Passive-heavy '被' construction leak
esl.why: Chinese marks the passive with 被 regardless of agency, so C1 writers overuse English passive even where an active voice is clearer.
esl.fix: Prefer active voice with a clear actor: 'I led the team'.

esl.title: 'When...then' literal translation
esl.why: English drops 'then' after 'when' in most cases; Chinese keeps 然后.
esl.fix: Drop 'then': 'When I arrived, I called...'.

esl.title: Over-long run-on sentence (no English clause boundary)
esl.why: Chinese allows very long sentences; English readers need clause boundaries. Missing periods in a C1 essay is a readability red flag.
esl.fix: Split into two or three sentences at natural clause boundaries.

esl.title: Article fully omitted (Russian has no article system)
esl.why: Russian has no grammatical article, so articles are omitted wholesale and the 'in the beginning / in the end' calque appears literally.
esl.fix: Drop the article where English requires none: 'go to university', 'in the beginning'.

esl.title: Preposition drift (case-driven in Russian)
esl.why: Russian case endings drive preposition choice; literal translations produce these over-specified prepositional phrases.
esl.fix: Use the natural English phrase: 'last week', 'in the morning', 'when'.

esl.title: Ser/estar tense mix-up (Spanish)
esl.why: Spanish verb conjugation merges 'ser/estar' usages; writers produce 'I am working since 2020' where English needs present perfect.
esl.fix: Fix the tense: 'I have worked since 2020', 'I am doing well'.

esl.title: 'Exactly for' / literal intensifier translation
esl.why: Spanish intensifier constructions translated literally produce 'exactly for'.
esl.fix: Use plain English: 'precisely because', 'specifically for'.

esl.title: Gerund overuse (Spanish/Portuguese)
esl.why: Spanish/Portuguese love gerunds; English prefers nouns or finite verbs here.
esl.fix: Use a noun or full verb: 'by solving', 'the solution'.

esl.title: Subject omitted (Japanese/Korean are pro-drop)
esl.why: Japanese and Korean omit subjects (pro-drop languages). In English a missing subject reads as broken rather than elegant.
esl.fix: Add the subject: 'It is very important to...'

esl.title: Copula missing after noun (Japanese/Korean)
esl.why: Japanese/Korean omit the copula; the English 'be' gets dropped after adjectives.
esl.fix: Add the copula: 'This is very important'.

esl.title: Hedging stacks weaken the sentence
esl.why: Two hedges in one clause. Native writers pick one and commit to a real verb.
esl.fix: Delete one hedge and replace the weak verb with a definite one.

esl.title: Vague 'make/do/get' instead of a precise verb
esl.pattern: \b(make a decision|do a research|make a progress|do an effort|make efforts|make an effort)\b
esl.why: 'Make/do' + noun is a calque of a common L1 construction. Use a precise verb.
esl.fix: Use the precise verb: decide / research / improve / attempt.

esl.title: 'Get + object' as a calque of 'receive/understand'
esl.why: Some L1s use a generic 'get' where English has a precise verb.
esl.fix: Use the precise verb: understand / realize.

esl.title: 'According to me' filler
esl.why: Direct translation of a common non-native phrase. English states the view directly.
esl.fix: Delete it, or attribute properly ('In my view' / 'According to X').

esl.title: 'In my opinion' on every claim
esl.why: Fine once, repetitive when it opens every paragraph -- an L1 essay habit.
esl.fix: Keep at most once; let the claim speak.

esl.title: Empty 'This is a very ...' opener
esl.why: Filler openers delay the point and read as non-native.
esl.fix: Lead with the concrete fact.

esl.title: 'I would like to' hedging opener
esl.why: Over-polite opener habit common in C1 academic writing.
esl.fix: Use a direct verb: 'I am applying', 'I thank you'.

esl.title: Comma splice (two clauses joined by a comma)
esl.why: A comma cannot join two independent clauses. A top-3 ESL error.
esl.fix: Use a period, semicolon, or a connector.

esl.title: Comma + 'and' joining two long independent clauses
esl.why: A light 'and' alone often produces a run-on in formal writing.
esl.fix: Use a semicolon, or split into two sentences.

esl.title: 'the' + fixed phrase that takes no article
esl.pattern: \b(in the university|in the company|in the school|in the beginning|in the end|in the last year|at the university|at the beginning)\b
esl.why: Fixed phrases do not take 'the'. One of the most reliable non-native tells.
esl.fix: Drop the article: at university, in the beginning, in the end.

esl.title: 'a' before an adjective missing its noun
esl.why: A 'to-infinitive' clause needs the article only if a noun follows; dropping it across the board is a common over-correction from ESL writers.
esl.fix: 'It is important to X' (no article) is correct; watch for over-insertion.

esl.title: 'Since/for + past' where present perfect is required
esl.why: Present perfect is required after 'since/for + duration'. Chinese/Russian writers keep present tense here.
esl.fix: Use present perfect: 'Since I have worked...'

esl.title: 'Must' for ordinary obligation
esl.why: Non-native writers overuse 'must' where 'have to' / 'should' / simple present is correct, overstating the obligation.
esl.fix: Downgrade to 'have to' (necessity) or 'should' (recommendation).

esl.title: 'Since I am graduate' (adjective/noun confusion)
esl.pattern: \bI am graduate\b|\bhe is student\b|\bshe is engineer\b|\bI am employee\b
esl.why: Some L1s drop the noun/verb inflection ('I am graduate' for 'I am a graduate').
esl.fix: Add the noun form or article: 'I am a graduate'.

esl.title: Double negative
esl.why: Negating an already-negative word is rare in standard English.
esl.fix: Use one negative: 'I don't know' / 'I know nothing'.

esl.title: 'more + comparative' redundancy
esl.why: Never double a comparative. A very visible ESL tell.
esl.fix: Use either 'more + long word' or the '-er' form.

esl.title: Intensifier stacking
esl.why: Native writing uses a single precise intensifier.
esl.fix: Use one stronger word.

esl.title: 'Very' before positive adjectives (needs a stronger word)
esl.why: Native writers avoid 'very + positive adjective' -- it reads childlike.
esl.fix: Use a stronger single word: excellent, crucial, compelling.

esl.title: Passive-heavy nominalization (reads stiff)
esl.why: Noun-heavy passives read stiffly in English application writing.
esl.fix: Use a verb: '... because it improved ...' not '... due to the improvement of ...'.

esl.title: 'Of course' used as filler
esl.why: Overused discourse marker in L1 writing.
esl.fix: Delete it or use a real connective.

esl.title: 'Pay attention' calque of 'please note'
esl.pattern: \bplease\s+(pay attention|note)\s+that\b|\bit should be noted that\b|\bplease be advised that\b
esl.why: Literal translation of a formal note phrase; reads as filler.
esl.fix: State the point directly.

esl.title: Translational connectives (chain)
esl.why: Mechanical transitional chains (translational habits) make writing read machine-translated.
esl.fix: Use plain connectors: 'Also', 'But', 'So'.

esl.title: 'Study knowledge' literal combination
esl.why: Direct translation of 'xuexi' / 'knowledge' collocations.
esl.fix: Use the natural pair: 'gain knowledge', 'study', 'learn about'.

esl.title: Verb agreement with the subject ('he/she/it' mismatch)
esl.why: Arabic/Urdu/Hebrew verbs inflect for person and number, so subject-verb agreement is automatic in the L1 and is easy to drop in English.
esl.fix: Match the verb to the subject: 'he IS', 'they ARE'.

esl.title: 'the' used where Arabic uses the definite article too freely
esl.why: Arabic definite article usage maps roughly but not exactly onto English 'the'; the transfer shows up as 'the' where English omits it.
esl.fix: English: 'at school', 'at work' (no article) in those senses.

esl.title: Missing present perfect where the L1 marks habituality
esl.why: Hindi/Urdu mark habitual or ongoing action with a perfective participle that English expresses with present perfect or simple present + 'always'.
esl.fix: Use present perfect: 'I have worked since 2020'.

esl.title: Case-driven word order carried into English
esl.why: Slavic languages mark case with endings, so word order is freer. The English result is repeated prepositional frames.
esl.fix: Use one preposition: 'about X' not 'about X about Y'.

esl.title: Article kept after a preposition (where English drops it)
esl.why: Case-driven languages still require an article after the preposition; English drops it in fixed phrases.
esl.fix: Drop it: 'at university', 'go home', 'at work'.

esl.title: Plural stacked with a noun already marked plural
esl.why: Vietnamese does not mark plural on the noun, so writers sometimes add -s where English already implies it.
esl.fix: Check whether the noun is already plural: 'many students' not 'many students s'.

esl.title: Turkish verb suffixes carried into English as separate words
esl.why: Turkish verb morphology attaches many suffixes that English expresses with separate words or tense markers.
esl.fix: Use English tense: 'he works', not 'he works meklar'.

esl.title: German separable-verb prefix left on the wrong side
esl.why: German separable verbs split the prefix; English keeps it attached.
esl.fix: Keep the prefix attached: 'started', not 'start ed up'.

esl.title: 'Ne ... pas' negation calque
esl.why: French wraps the negative with ne...pas; English uses a single negative.
esl.fix: One negative: 'I do not know', never 'I do not know not'.

esl.title: Fragment sentence (no main verb)
esl.why: A clause starting with a subordinator needs a main verb to finish the sentence. Fragment sentences read as broken to native ears.
esl.fix: Complete the sentence: add a subject and main verb.

esl.title: Two sentences run together with no punctuation
esl.why: A string of past participles with no main verb is a very common non-native pattern, especially in applicant CVs.
esl.fix: Add a main verb and punctuation: 'I designed, built and shipped...'.

esl.title: Missing conjunction between two verbs
esl.why: English needs a conjunction between coordinated verbs.
esl.fix: Insert 'and' / 'then': 'I designed and built...'.

esl.title: Subject-verb agreement ('is' with plural)
esl.why: Basic agreement is the one thing every grammar checker should catch; if it is still wrong, the pattern is worth a dedicated pass.
esl.fix: they ARE / it IS.

esl.title: Article before an uncountable abstract noun used wrongly
esl.why: Abstract uncountable nouns normally take no article.
esl.fix: Drop 'the': 'the advice' -> 'advice'.

esl.title: 'most + est' redundancy
esl.why: Never double the superlative.
esl.fix: Use 'most' + long word or '-est', not both.

esl.title: 'There is' with a plural noun
esl.why: Agreement again, but extremely common in non-native writing.
esl.fix: Use 'there ARE many'.

esl.title: 'Could of' / 'would of' / 'should of'
esl.why: Non-native writers hear 'could have' and write 'of'. One of the most recognisable ESL written errors.
esl.fix: Use 'have': 'could have written'.

esl.title: 'less' with a countable plural noun
esl.why: Countable plurals take 'fewer'; only uncountables take 'less'.
esl.fix: Use 'fewer'.

esl.title: 'Affect' used as a noun
esl.why: 'Affect' is the verb; 'effect' is the noun. Frequent L1 transfer.
esl.fix: Use 'the effect of' / 'in effect'.

esl.title: Its written without apostrophe when possessive
esl.why: Possessive 'its' takes no apostrophe; 'it's' means 'it is'.
esl.fix: Use 'its' (no apostrophe) for possession.

esl.title: 'Alot' as one word
esl.why: 'A lot' is two words; 'alot' is not a word.
esl.fix: Write 'a lot'.

esl.title: Overuse of 'which' where 'that' is required
esl.why: English restricts with 'that' and adds with 'which'. Non-native writers often attach every clause with 'which'.
esl.fix: Use 'that' for defining clauses.

esl.title: Comma splice after a colon
esl.why: A colon introduces a clause; joining it with a comma is redundant.
esl.fix: Drop the comma after a colon.

esl.title: Apostrophe on plural nouns
esl.why: Plurals never take an apostrophe.
esl.fix: Drop the apostrophe: 'students' work'.

esl.title: 'Very much' used as an intensifier before an adjective
esl.why: Use 'very' alone before adjectives, or a stronger single word.
esl.fix: Use 'very important' or 'crucial'.

esl.title: 'In order to' where 'to' suffices (formal register)
esl.why: Not wrong, but often reads stiffly in an application essay.
esl.fix: Prefer 'to' — shorter and more direct.

esl.title: 'At this point in time' filler
esl.why: Filler phrase common in non-native formal writing.
esl.fix: Say 'now' or 'currently'.

esl.title: 'Due to the fact that' filler
esl.why: Verbose calque of a single preposition.
esl.fix: Use 'because'.

esl.title: 'Each other' used for singular pairs
esl.why: 'Each other' is for two; 'everyone' is for three or more.
esl.fix: Use 'each other' for two, 'one another' otherwise.

esl.title: 'Many times' where 'often' is meant
esl.why: Literal translation of a frequentative adverb.
esl.fix: Use 'often' or 'frequently'.

esl.title: 'Since' vs 'for' duration confusion
esl.why: 'for' + duration, 'since' + point in time. The pairing is a frequent slip.
esl.fix: 'for three years', 'since 2020'.

esl.title: 'Amount of' with a countable noun
esl.why: 'Amount of' takes uncountables; 'number of' takes countables.
esl.fix: Use 'number of' for countable nouns.

esl.title: 'Succeed to do'
esl.why: English uses 'succeed in doing' or just 'succeed'.
esl.fix: Use 'succeeded in doing' / 'succeeded'.

esl.title: 'Explain me' calque
esl.why: Direct translation of a Romance/Germanic calque; English uses the interrogative or a that-clause.
esl.fix: Use 'explain to me' or 'can you explain'.

esl.title: 'Most speak English' missing 'of them' / 'people'
esl.why: Needs an explicit subject: 'most applicants speak'.
esl.fix: Add the subject: 'most applicants'.

esl.title: 'Of about' / 'around of' / 'approximately of'
esl.why: Double preposition, a very visible calque.
esl.fix: Use one: 'about', 'around', 'approximately'.

esl.title: Comma before 'and' inside a short phrase
esl.why: No comma before 'and' joining two short items in a simple list.
esl.fix: Drop the comma.

esl.title: Article used with unique/singular identification
esl.why: English drops the article with unique/only/main identifiers.
esl.fix: Drop 'the': 'the only way' -> 'the only way' is fine, but 'a unique tool' not 'the unique tool'.

esl.title: Past tense where the situation is still ongoing
esl.why: If the action continues now, English requires the present perfect.
esl.fix: Use 'I have lived here since 2020'.

esl.title: 'will' in an application essay where past is meant
esl.why: Applications describe what you have done, not what you will do.
esl.fix: Use past tense for completed work.

esl.title: Second person ('you') in a personal statement
esl.why: A statement of purpose is first person. 'You' belongs in outreach emails, not in essays.
esl.fix: Rewrite in first person.
